presentingComplaint: Six weeks of daily evening fever, drenching night sweats and 9 kg weight loss, now with worsening breathlessness and confusion.
history: Migrant construction worker from eastern Uttar Pradesh, resident in a crowded urban settlement. HIV-positive, diagnosed 8 months ago, poorly adherent to antiretrovirals (last CD4 unknown). Treated for smear-positive pulmonary TB 14 months ago at a private clinic but self-discontinued the intensive-phase regimen after 6 weeks when he felt better — a classic incomplete/interrupted prior treatment history. His brother, also on TB treatment, was recently confirmed to have rifampicin-resistant disease on Xpert. Over 6 weeks he has had low-grade evening-predominant fever, soaking night sweats, anorexia and marked weight loss, with a dry cough for the last 3 weeks. In the past 4 days he has become increasingly breathless at rest and, per family, intermittently drowsy and disoriented.
examination: Cachectic, ill and toxic-looking young man. Temperature 38.9°C, visibly tachypnoeic. Oral thrush present. No neck rigidity but GCS fluctuating (E3V4M6). Fundoscopy shows two pale, raised choroidal tubercles — a specific sign of haematogenous dissemination. Firm, non-tender hepatomegaly 4 cm and splenomegaly 3 cm below costal margins. Fine bilateral inspiratory crepitations throughout both lung fields. No focal neurological deficit; generalized lymphadenopathy of small, firm cervical and axillary nodes.

labs.note: Pancytopenia with markedly raised ESR/LDH and cholestatic LFT pattern typical of marrow and hepatic granulomatous involvement in miliary TB.

imaging: Chest radiograph shows innumerable 1-3 mm nodules uniformly distributed throughout both lung fields — the classic miliary pattern. High-resolution CT chest confirms random-distribution micronodularity with early bilateral ground-glass change. Abdominal ultrasound: hepatosplenomegaly with multiple hypoechoic microabscesses in spleen and para-aortic nodal enlargement. CT/MRI brain unremarkable; CSF (given fluctuating sensorium) shows lymphocytic pleocytosis (WBC 90, 85% lymphocytes), protein 1.1 g/L, glucose ratio 0.4 — consistent with early meningeal seeding.
microbiology: Sputum and CSF Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra: MTB detected, high burden, RIFAMPICIN RESISTANCE DETECTED. AFB smear (sputum) 2+. Line-probe assay (second-line): additional resistance to fluoroquinolones NOT detected; isoniazid resistance (katG) confirmed. Blood mycobacterial culture and bone-marrow aspirate culture both grew M. tuberculosis complex; phenotypic DST confirms MDR-TB (resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin, susceptible to fluoroquinolones, bedaquiline, linezolid). Blood bacterial cultures sterile. HIV viral load high.
differentialDiagnoses: Pyrexia of unknown origin from another disseminated infection
finalDiagnosis: Disseminated (miliary) tuberculosis with meningeal seeding in an HIV-coinfected host, caused by multidrug-resistant (rifampicin/isoniazid-resistant) M. tuberculosis, requiring escalation to a second-line regimen.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Tuberculosis (Mycobacterial Diseases)
WHO — Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis: Drug-Resistant TB Treatment — 2022
India NTEP — Guidelines for Programmatic Management of Drug-Resistant TB (PMDT) — 2021
stewardship: This is not a conventional antibacterial-stewardship problem but a drug-resistant TB escalation problem. Empiric first-line therapy would be four-drug HRZE, but two high-risk features — prior interrupted TB treatment and a confirmed rifampicin-resistant household contact — mandate rapid molecular DST (Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra) BEFORE committing, exactly as done here. With rifampicin resistance confirmed, standard HRZE is abandoned and the patient is escalated to a WHO-concordant all-oral MDR-TB regimen (bedaquiline + linezolid + levofloxacin + clofazimine + cycloserine; BPaLM is contraindicated here because of concurrent CNS/meningeal disease, which requires a longer regimen with CNS-penetrating agents). Fluoroquinolone susceptibility on line-probe assay is what makes levofloxacin usable. 'Source control' in disseminated TB means securing microbiological diagnosis from multiple compartments (sputum, CSF, blood, marrow) and controlling the immunosuppressive driver — start/optimise ART after 2 weeks of TB therapy to reduce paradoxical IRIS, with corticosteroids given the meningeal involvement. Baseline ECG (QTc — bedaquiline/clofazimine/moxifloxacin), visual acuity/colour vision, and audiometry are monitored; contact tracing and notification are mandatory public-health steps.
contraindications: Do not use standard HRZE / rifampicin-based regimen once rifampicin resistance is confirmed
Avoid BPaLM short regimen with CNS/meningeal TB — insufficient CNS penetration; use a longer regimen
Caution combining bedaquiline + clofazimine + fluoroquinolone (additive QT prolongation) — serial ECG monitoring
Linezolid: monitor for myelosuppression (already pancytopenic) and peripheral/optic neuropathy
Do not start full-dose ART simultaneously — delay ~2 weeks to reduce IRIS risk, but do not withhold TB therapy
edgeCases: Paradoxical worsening (IRIS) after ART initiation may mimic treatment failure
Pancytopenia may be marrow TB rather than drug toxicity — bone-marrow findings help distinguish
Choroidal tubercles are pathognomonic and can secure a bedside diagnosis before culture
Hyponatraemia may reflect SIADH from CNS/pulmonary TB or coexisting adrenal TB (adrenal crisis mimic)
expectedMaiK: Recognise miliary/disseminated TB clinically (chronic constitutional symptoms + miliary CXR + choroidal tubercles + organomegaly in an immunocompromised host) and, given prior interrupted treatment and an MDR contact, act on molecular DST to escalate from first-line HRZE to a WHO-concordant longer MDR-TB regimen with CNS cover, while managing HIV coinfection and monitoring drug toxicity.
